reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Statistics & Visualization
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 13. Statistics helps us summarize evidence, and visualization helps us communicate patterns in a form people can understand quickly.

We’ll work with center, spread, distributions, group comparisons, correlation, uncertainty, and basic visual choices.

[tts-break]

The most important habit is interpretation. A statistic is useful only when we can explain what it means in the context of the data.

slides.title: How to use this page
slides.transcript:
Before running each example, think about the question being answered.

Are we describing a typical value? Comparing groups? Looking for a relationship? Measuring uncertainty? Choosing a visual?

[tts-break]

Then run the code and explain the result in plain language. That translation from output to interpretation is the core skill in this module.

slides.title: Learning path for Module 13
slides.transcript:
We’ll begin with descriptive statistics such as mean and median, then look at distributions and group comparisons.

Next comes correlation, followed by a simple introduction to confidence intervals. We’ll finish by matching visual forms to analytical questions and building a short statistical report.

[tts-break]

Think of the sequence as summarize, compare, relate, quantify uncertainty, and communicate.

slides.title: Descriptive statistics
slides.transcript:
Let’s summarize a small set of scores.

The mean gives the arithmetic average. The median gives the middle value after ordering the data. Minimum and maximum define the observed range, while standard deviation describes how spread out the values are around the mean.

[tts-break]

No single statistic tells the whole story. Mean and median can respond differently to extreme values, and spread matters even when two datasets have the same average.

Run the cell, then change one score to an extreme value and see which statistics move the most.

slides.title: Distribution with bins
slides.transcript:
A distribution tells us how values are spread across ranges.

The code places each number into a bin such as forty to forty-nine or fifty to fifty-nine. The number of hash marks represents how many values fall into that interval.

[tts-break]

This is the same basic idea as a histogram, just displayed with text instead of graphical bars.

Look for where the values concentrate and whether the frequencies are balanced or uneven across the ranges.

slides.title: Compare groups
slides.transcript:
Grouped summaries help us compare categories using the same statistics.

The DataFrame contains scores for groups A and B. Groupby separates the records, and agg calculates count, mean, median, and standard deviation for each group.

[tts-break]

Compare both center and spread. A higher mean does not automatically mean every observation in that group is higher.

Group summaries are a starting point for comparison, not a complete explanation of why groups differ.

slides.title: Correlation
slides.transcript:
Correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two numeric variables.

Here hours studied increases as score increases, so we expect a strong positive correlation. A value close to one indicates a strong positive linear relationship.

[tts-break]

But correlation does not prove causation. Two variables can move together because of other factors, reverse direction, or coincidence.

Use correlation as evidence of association, not as proof that one variable causes the other.

slides.title: Simple confidence interval idea
slides.transcript:
A sample mean is an estimate of a larger population quantity, and estimates have uncertainty.

The code calculates the sample mean, standard deviation, standard error, and then an approximate ninety-five percent interval using one point nine six times the standard error.

[tts-break]

The interval gives a range of plausible values around the estimate under the assumptions of this simplified method.

At this stage, focus on the idea: a single sample statistic should not be treated as perfectly precise.

slides.title: Choose the right visual
slides.transcript:
The best visual depends on the question.

Bar charts compare categories. Line charts emphasize change over time. Histograms show distributions. Box plots compare spread across groups. Scatter plots show relationships between two numeric variables. Tables are useful when exact values matter.

[tts-break]

Do not choose a chart because it looks impressive. Choose the form that makes the analytical question easiest to answer.

slides.title: Text-based bar chart
slides.transcript:
Even without a plotting library, we can demonstrate the logic of a bar chart.

The dictionary stores counts for web, email, and store. Repeating the block character creates a bar whose length matches the count.

[tts-break]

Web has the longest bar because it has twelve observations, followed by email with seven and store with four.

The visual encoding is simple: larger values produce longer bars.

slides.title: Mini statistics report
slides.transcript:
A useful report combines numerical summaries with a sentence a reader can understand.

The code calculates mean, median, minimum, maximum, and overall spread. Then f-strings turn those results into two short statements.

[tts-break]

This is a good reporting habit. Do not dump raw statistical output when a concise interpretation can communicate the result more clearly.

Always keep the wording tied to what the statistic actually supports.

slides.title: Module 13 wrap-up
slides.transcript:
Let’s bring the ideas together.

Mean and median describe center. Range and standard deviation describe spread. Frequencies help describe a distribution. Grouped statistics support comparisons. Correlation describes linear association, and confidence intervals remind us that estimates contain uncertainty.

[tts-break]

Good visualization and reporting connect those statistics back to the question the audience actually cares about.

[tts-break]

Module 14 brings many of the course ideas together in an introductory machine learning workflow. We’ll read data, separate features from a target, create training and testing sets, train a simple model, evaluate its predictions, compare it with a baseline, and discuss issues such as data leakage and responsible interpretation.
